content: 1. Drug Treatment and Nutritional Therapy in Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM): Initiate nutritional therapy while withholding antiretroviral drug treatment for one to two weeks during the stabilization phase. Alternatively, delay antiretroviral therapy until the rehabilitation phase is reached. Outcomes to monitor include mortality rates, markers of nutritional status (e.g., lean body mass, height gain, body weight, weight-for-height, weight-for-age, body mass index, and mid-upper arm circumference), improvements in CD4 percentage and counts, viral load, tolerance to antiretroviral drugs (including adverse effects), and adherence to antiretroviral therapy. 2. Management of HIV-Infected Children with Severe Acute Malnutrition: For children aged 0–59 months with severe acute malnutrition and HIV, assess whether antiretroviral drug dosing should be adjusted compared to non-malnourished children of the same weight. Compare pharmacokinetics (e.g., peak levels, clearance) of antiretroviral drugs between malnourished and non-malnourished children of the same age and weight. Outcomes to evaluate include drug tolerance, adverse events, mortality, pharmacokinetic measures, drug absorption, nutritional status markers, and changes in CD4 counts during the first three months of treatment. 3. Admission and Discharge Criteria for Infants Under 6 Months with SAM: Admission criteria include mid-upper arm circumference, chest circumference, head circumference, weight loss, breastfeeding failure, and weight-for-length measurements. Discharge criteria differ from those for older children and may include weight gain of 15–20% after oedema resolution or weight-for-height exceeding -1 standard deviation. Outcomes to monitor include short-term mortality, recovery rates, weight gain, adverse effects, time to recovery, resource utilization, and restoration of exclusive breastfeeding. 4. Feeding Severely Malnourished Infants Under 6 Months: For infants aged 0–6 months, assess the effectiveness of different feeding approaches, including breast milk substitutes, expressed breast milk, animal milk, and therapeutic formulas such as F-75 and F-100. Outcomes include mortality, recovery rates, weight gain, diarrheal episodes, restoration of exclusive breastfeeding, time to recovery, length gain, adverse effects, and breast milk output. 5. Research Priorities in SAM Management: Refine mid-upper arm circumference cut-off values for identifying SAM in children aged 6–59 months and assess treatment outcomes. Evaluate the validity of mid-upper arm circumference versus weight-for-height Z-scores as discharge criteria and determine appropriate thresholds. Investigate the sensitivity and specificity of mid-upper arm circumference measurements across age ranges and in the presence of stunting or oedema. Assess the correlation between anthropometric indicators and mortality risk or treatment response in infants under 6 months and children over 5 years, particularly in high and low HIV prevalence settings. 6. Fluid Management in SAM: Compare the efficacy and safety of ReSoMal (rehydration solution for malnourished children) versus standard oral rehydration solutions in severely malnourished, dehydrated children with non-cholera diarrhea. Determine the most appropriate fluid strategies (type, volume, rate) and monitoring approaches for managing severe dehydration or shock in children with SAM, with or without oedema. Improve diagnostic methods for assessing dehydration severity and differentiating types of shock (e.g., hypovolemic, septic, cardiogenic) to guide management. 7. Vitamin A Supplementation in SAM: Compare the efficacy of daily low-dose vitamin A supplementation versus single high-dose supplementation in children with SAM, particularly those with bilateral pitting oedema, severe diarrhea, or shigellosis. Investigate strategies to improve and sustain vitamin A status post-treatment and assess regional differences in response and safety. 8. Therapeutic Feeding Approaches in SAM: Evaluate the efficacy of different ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs) that meet WHO specifications and are made from various ingredients in different regions. Compare the effectiveness of RUTFs and F-100 therapeutic milk in children with SAM and diarrhea. Assess the impact of transitioning from F-75 to RUTF or F-100 to RUTF before hospital discharge and continued outpatient care. 9. Management of HIV-Infected Children with SAM: Investigate whether early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (after stabilization of metabolic complications and treatment of sepsis) improves outcomes and reduces adverse events compared to later initiation. Assess pharmacokinetic differences in antiretroviral drugs in HIV-infected children with and without SAM and determine if dose adjustments are necessary to avoid toxicity or ensure therapeutic levels. Evaluate the most effective therapeutic feeding approaches for HIV-infected children with SAM and persistent diarrhea. 10. Identifying and Managing Infants Under 6 Months with SAM: Determine the predictive value of population-derived thresholds for weight-for-height, mid-upper arm circumference, and growth velocity in identifying high-risk infants. Assess the safety and effectiveness of therapeutic feeding approaches, including breastfeeding and supplementary feeding methods, for infants under 6 months with SAM. Investigate whether infants with weight-for-length below -3 Z-scores also exhibit reduced growth velocity and how this impacts management. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the guidelines and research priorities for managing severe acute malnutrition in infants and children, with a focus on evidence-based interventions and outcomes.
